gender_fit: Neutral. Palettes run from earthy to slate to night, and the motif comes from the person's own world.
when_it_makes_sense: A nature, garden, birdwatching or hiking person, or anyone whose habits are worth 'studying'.\nA warm, witty card for a partner or parent where a loud roast would feel wrong.\nAdult and senior recipients: readable serif type, slow pace, no dexterity needed.
example_card_a: Ren, 41, cyclist and coffee obsessive, from friends. Night Survey palette; Cormorant Garamond + Lora + IBM Plex Mono; range map with pinned sightings; tools-as-fauna motif; pin drop; tick sightings. Binomial 'Velocipedus caffeinatus'. Reads as a dark, dry survey of a rare bike-café species.
example_card_b: Nan, 78, gardener, from her grandchildren. Herbarium Sepia palette; IM Fell English + Libre Baskerville; facing pages; botanical motif; ink draw-on; turn a page corner. Binomial 'Nana hortensis'. Reads as a pressed-flower keepsake. Differs from Ren's card on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Obsession or habit: the specimen subject and the Latin pun.
Place they live in or love: the habitat plate and range map.
Age: the edition number and reading level.
Tone: how dry the annotations are.
Number of photos: plates versus field photographs.
Favourite setting or colour: palette.
fixed_dna:
Every scene is a numbered plate or page with a caption block and a margin note.
The recipient is catalogued under an invented binomial name (a pun on their name and a habit).
Art is one-colour line or wash drawing in inline SVG. Photos, if any, sit as mounted 'field photographs'.
Unhurried pacing: pages settle, nothing bounces.
watch_outs: Drawings must be simple, template-built SVG: never promise realistic illustration. Every Latin pun needs a gloss line. Skip animals the recipient dislikes and any 'species' joke about body or health. Marginalia are decoration: keep them short.

gender_fit: Neutral in structure but often read as male-coded. Re-skin with Amber Terminal, Ultraviolet or Paper Tape, and build the modules from the person's own hobbies rather than gadgets.
when_it_makes_sense: Tech-minded friends, gamers and engineers.\nAffectionate adult roasts and any recipient who likes mock-serious documents.\nA card that should feel closest to Jordan.EXE.
example_card_a: Sam, 16, gamer, from a best friend. Ultraviolet palette; VT323 + Share Tech Mono; full-screen console; pixel icons motif; typed lines; press any key. Device 'SAM-OS 16.0'.
example_card_b: Priya, 34, project lead, from her team. Paper Tape palette; DM Mono + Syne; stamped document on the desk; stamps and barcodes; snap cut; hold to run a diagnostic. 'Unit PRIYA-34: overcommitted, still shipping.' Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Profession or hobby: module names.
Habits: warnings and error codes.
Age: the version number.
Tone: severity words (roast says WARNING, warm says ADVISORY).
Love of retro tech: CRT texture option.
Their name: the device name.
fixed_dna:
Starts with a boot sequence and a tap or key gate.
Information alternates between huge statements, diagnostic panels and stamped documents.
Monospace metadata on everything (edition label, timestamps, status codes), one controlled accent and one warning colour.
Short, purposeful transitions. No continuous flicker.
watch_outs: Flicker can trigger photosensitivity: nothing flashing more than 3 times a second, and honour reduced-motion. Monospace is tiring past a few lines, so long copy uses the text face. No fake warnings about real security, money or health.

gender_fit: Neutral. Fantasy, space and cosy worlds are all in the kit. The hero's class and pronouns come from the giver.
when_it_makes_sense: Kids 9 to 12 and teens who game.\nAdults who play tabletop or video games.\nA milestone that feels like levelling up, or a birthday for the hero of a friend group.
example_card_a: Riley, 9, space and a rabbit called Bean, from a parent. Star Chart palette; Fredoka + Nunito; quest board; stars-and-planets motif; sparkle pickup; collect three stars. Class 'Rabbit Ranger', level 9.
example_card_b: Dev, 45, tabletop player, from his group. Parchment & Ember palette; Cinzel + Lora; journal spread; runes-and-borders motif; scroll unroll; accept a quest. Class 'Dungeon Master of Snacks'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Main hobby: the hero's class.
Obsessions and objects: inventory items.
Catchphrases: dialogue lines.
The giver: the companion.
Age: level, and how much reading fits in each dialogue box.
What they love (fantasy, space, cosy): the world.
fixed_dna:
A hero sheet (name, class, level equal to age, three to five stats) opens the card and returns at the end with 'level up'.
Scenes are quests with an objective and a reward (badge, item or title).
Dialogue boxes carry the giver's voice as a companion character.
Every activity is skippable. Scores are session results, never claims about their life.
watch_outs: Stat numbers are jokes, never measurements: do not rank weight, looks or money. Keep games skippable and untimed for under 9s. Invent the world: no third-party creatures, spells or names. Dialogue boxes need a text-size floor so reading stays comfortable.

gender_fit: Neutral. Paper colours span kraft, rose, sage, linen and evening.
when_it_makes_sense: Parents, partners and quieter friends: anyone for whom a roast would feel wrong.\nMilestones such as a 50th, a retirement or a first birthday away from home.\nPhoto-rich briefs, or no-photo briefs that are all memories.
example_card_a: Mum, 70, from her children. Kraft & Ink palette; Fraunces + Source Serif 4 + Caveat; open box with objects fanned; ticket stubs and stamps; lid lift; unfold the note. Objects: a crossword clipping, a bus ticket to the seaside, a recipe card.
example_card_b: Tom, 30, from his partner. Evening Box palette; Instrument Serif + Inter; timeline strip of small objects; keys and trinkets; slide out and settle; arrange three items. Objects: the front-door key, a concert wristband, a shopping list. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Real photos and objects: the box contents.
Places and years: labels on the objects.
How close the giver is: how personal the handwritten touches get.
Fewer than 3 photos: designed objects (tickets, recipes, maps) fill the box.
Favourite colour: the accent.
Age: text size.
fixed_dna:
A lid or opening gesture starts the card. The last object is always the real letter.
Each scene is a physical-feeling object with subtle depth (paper grain, soft shadow, a fold).
Editorial serif headings, clean body text, one restrained accent. Handwriting is decoration only, never body copy.
Nothing loud: one gentle surprise per scene at most.
watch_outs: A private letter must not auto-share: the share tile is a separate approval. Photos of children or third parties need the giver's consent. Handwriting fonts hurt legibility, so decoration only. The no-photo box must be as rich as the photo one.

gender_fit: Neutral. The palette comes from the person's own favourites, so pink, cobalt and lilac are equally available.
when_it_makes_sense: Outgoing friends and big milestones (30, 40, 50).\nMusic, art and fashion lovers.\nA card meant to be shared on social feeds.
example_card_a: Jo, 40, musician, from friends. Cobalt Pop palette; Abril Fatface + Poppins; giant numeral; circles and arches; scale pop; tap to reveal. Poster: 'FORTY. STILL THE PLOT TWIST.'
example_card_b: Mira, 7, dinosaurs and pink, from a parent. Pink Punch palette; Bowlby One + Figtree; stacked words; stars and bursts; colour wipe; flip the award. Poster: 'SEVEN. ROAR.' Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Age or milestone: the giant numeral.
Favourite colours: the palette.
Taste in music, food or films: the taste-profile poster.
Best-known trait: the 'main character' poster title.
Number of scenes: how compositions rotate.
fixed_dna:
Each scene is a full-bleed poster with one dominant graphic idea (a huge numeral, a shape, a headline).
A tight palette of 3 to 4 saturated colours holds every scene together. Scenes change composition, not colour.
Oversized type plus one short line of small print per scene.
Every scene is designed as a shareable tile first.
watch_outs: Saturated fields make small text fail contrast fast: keep body copy on the ink colour and check every scene. Giant numerals and short lines must survive long names. Stay at 4 colours or the scenes stop feeling like one card. Avoid look-alikes of real brands' posters and logos.

gender_fit: Neutral. Ferric, chrome, neon and mint palettes cover the range.
when_it_makes_sense: Music lovers, musicians and DJs, and friends with a shared soundtrack.\nCards that include a made-for-them song, voice notes or beat pads.\nRecipients who remember tapes, or who simply like the look.
example_card_a: Jamie, 40, from friends. Ferric Brown palette; Permanent Marker + Space Mono; cassette front with a J-card; cassette-reel motif; reel spin; press play. Track 3: 'Ten Minutes Out (Extended)'.
example_card_b: Zoe, 15, from her brother. Neon Side B palette; Bebas Neue + Courier Prime; playlist screen with cover thumbnails; waveforms and EQ bars; EQ bounce; tap the pads. Track 4: 'Sorry I Ate Your Fries'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Music taste and era: the medium and label art.
A song they love (title only, never lyrics): the cover inspiration.
Catchphrases: track titles.
Age: the year on the label.
Number of voices: 'featuring' credits.
The giver's tone: J-card lettering.
fixed_dna:
Opens on the cassette (or sleeve or playlist) with a title and a tracklist. Each scene is a numbered track with a title and a duration.
The transport buttons are the navigation: play, next and back.
Liner notes (short credits and a dedication) close the card.
Every track has a visual fallback because sound is opt-in.
watch_outs: Sound needs an opt-in and a full visual fallback. Synthesized tracks need a sensible volume and length. Never reproduce lyrics or a real recording. Cassettes and vinyl mean little to some kids, so the playlist layout is the fallback.

gender_fit: Neutral. Pixel worlds read 'gamer' by default: use Candy Cabinet or Sunset Sprite palettes and sprites from the person's own interests (pets, baking, dance).
when_it_makes_sense: Gamers of any age and kids who like simple games.\nRetro-loving adults and friend groups with in-jokes to turn into bosses.\nCards that lean on games (Catch Game, Tap Challenge, Perfect Timing).
example_card_a: Sam, 16, from friends. Cabinet Night palette; Silkscreen + Pixelify Sans; attract screen; pixel icons of favourite things; sprite bob; insert coin. 'LEVEL 3: GROUP CHAT'.
example_card_b: Ada, 8, cats and pizza, from her dad. Candy Cabinet palette; Pixelify Sans + DM Mono; level-select map; coins, stars and hearts; score count-up; pick a level. 'LEVEL 2: PIZZA CAT'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Favourite things: sprites (simple 16 by 16 icons) and level names.
Catchphrases: boss lines.
Age: starting level and score.
Consoles and eras they loved: grid size and colour limit.
Giver and friends: the other high-score initials.
fixed_dna:
Starts on an attract screen (logo and a blinking start prompt) and ends on a high-score table with the recipient first.
Pixel art on a fixed low-resolution grid, scaled with crisp edges. Headings in pixel fonts.
Scenes are levels on a level-select screen, each with a title card.
Games are tiny, forgiving and skippable. Lives never run out.
watch_outs: Games are forgiving, skippable, untimed for under 9s and never end in 'game over'. No recognisable characters, mazes or mechanics from real games. Pixel fonts are hard to read at length: body copy uses the text face. No screen flashing.

gender_fit: Neutral by design: the sport comes from the person's own life (or is invented) and colours are plain. The loud broadcast voice is a tone choice, not part of the theme.
when_it_makes_sense: Sports fans and players, and team-mates or coaches giving a card.\nFriends who compete about everything (board games, quizzes, fantasy leagues).\nRetirements and 'career highlight' birthdays.
example_card_a: Rob, 50, weekend footballer, from his team. Grass & Chalk palette; Anton + Inter; broadcast frame with lower thirds; field markings; ticker crawl; vote the player of the match. Position: 'Left back, mostly stationary'.
example_card_b: Lena, 12, swimmer, from her family. Ice Rink palette; Big Shoulders Display + DM Sans; line-up card; whistle, stopwatch and medal icons; lower-third slide; kick off. 'Career best: 50 m freestyle, one snack break'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Sport they play or watch: vocabulary and field graphics (or an invented sport).
Role in the group: their position.
Habits: career 'stats'.
Giver and friends: the roster.
Age: the season number.
Their team's colours: used as plain colours, never crests.
fixed_dna:
Opens with a broadcast-style intro and closes on a final scoreboard where the giver's side wins.
One ticker or scoreboard strip carries short lines through every scene.
Stats, line-ups and replays are the core formats: numbers and short labels beat paragraphs.
Invented teams, leagues and colours only: never real clubs, crests or players.
watch_outs: No real clubs, crests, leagues, players or famous commentators' catchphrases. Stat jokes are never about body, health or money. Keep sound opt-in and limit the ticker to one moving element.

gender_fit: Neutral. The character kit is built from what the giver says, so any hair, clothes or pronouns work. The hero is never assumed.
when_it_makes_sense: Kids 6 to 12 and teens who love cartoons and graphic novels.\nStory-heavy cards: an anecdote told in panels, or an 'origin story' for a milestone.\nFriend groups with a running gag.
example_card_a: Kai, 11, dinosaurs and skateboarding, from his sister. Sunday Funnies palette; Luckiest Guy + Patrick Hand; six-panel page; speed lines and impact bursts; bubble pop-in; tap to reveal the next panel. Issue #11: 'The Kid Who Never Landed It (Yet)'.
example_card_b: Marcus, 38, ex-drummer, from his bandmates. Noir Ink palette; Bebas Neue + Special Elite; splash page with one big panel; ink splatter and cross-hatch; page turn with a curl; choose the sound effect. Issue #38: 'One More Encore'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Appearance details the giver volunteers (hair, glasses, favourite hoodie): the character kit. Never guessed.
Hobbies and memories: the origin story.
Catchphrase: the recurring bubble.
The giver: the sidekick.
Tone: genre (adventure, sci-fi, noir, slice-of-life).
fixed_dna:
Every scene is a page or spread of panels with gutters. Captions and bubbles carry the text, and the text is live.
A cover (issue number equal to the age, or the years known) opens the card. A 'next issue' teaser closes it.
Ink line, halftone and lettered sound effects. Structure comes from panels, not from single-idea posters, which keeps it apart from Technicolour.
Characters are original cartoon figures built from a simple parts kit, never a known character.
watch_outs: Never draw the recipient's body from a guess: volunteered details only, and nothing about weight or looks. No known characters, costumes, logos or trademarked sound effects. Bubble text stays live and at least 16 px on phones. Character art is the costly part: fall back to icon-and-initial avatars until the kit exists.

gender_fit: Neutral. The site picks colours from what the child loves and never defaults to pink for girls or blue for boys.
when_it_makes_sense: Kids 3 to 8 from a parent, grandparent or older sibling.\nA first birthday, or a milestone such as a first year at school or a new baby sister.\nA grown-up who wants to read it aloud together.
example_card_a: Theo, 4, trucks and a stuffed bear called Bruno, from his grandparents. Sunny Day palette; Baloo 2 + Quicksand; full-page picture with a text band; toys and blocks; bounce-in characters; tap anywhere to turn the page. Refrain: 'And Theo said, VROOM!'
example_card_b: Ines, 7, the sea and a first swimming badge, from her dad. Sea Glass palette; Grandstander + Patrick Hand; spot illustration with a rhyme couplet; sea and boats; gentle sway; lift the flap. Refrain: 'One more splash for Ines!' Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Age: line length and vocabulary (picture-first for 4 to 8).
Favourite animal, colour or toy: the companion and palette.
A milestone (first year at school, new sibling, lost tooth): the plot.
Place: the setting.
Who reads: read-aloud mode with word highlighting when a grown-up will read.
fixed_dna:
Every scene is a picture-book spread: one large illustration area, three short lines at most, and a refrain that returns ('...and that was Theo!').
The recipient is the hero, drawn as a simple original character. The giver appears as a helper.
Big controls: Next and Back at least 56 px, plus tap anywhere to turn the page.
Rhythm and repetition, never sarcasm.
watch_outs: Child-appropriate content rules apply whatever the theme: nothing scary, no teasing. Keep illustration simple and original with template shapes, because generated faces look uncanny. Recorded voice and photos of children need the giver's consent. Tap targets at least 56 px.

gender_fit: Neutral. The default sticker look can read girl-coded: use sports, space, dinosaur or gadget sets and the Night Sticker or Sky Pool palettes when the child asks for them.
when_it_makes_sense: Kids 4 to 12 and teens who collect things.\nCrafty, journalling friends and relatives.\nCards with many small facts and few photos.
example_card_a: Maya, 6, dogs and pancakes, from her aunt. Bubblegum Dots palette; Chewy + DM Sans; sticker sheet beside the page; animals and pets; wiggle on placement; drag stickers onto the page.
example_card_b: Leo, 14, skater and ramen fan, from his cousin. Night Sticker palette; Caveat Brush + Work Sans; bullet-journal grid; sports and hobby gear; slide from the tray; tap to place the next sticker. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Every fact: one sticker.
Favourites: the sticker set.
Age: sticker size and how many to place (fewer when younger).
Favourite colours: palette.
Photos: die-cut 'photo stickers'.
The giver's handwriting style: the note.
fixed_dna:
Every scene is a page with a sticker tray. Each sticker is one real fact (an icon and a short label) that reveals a line when placed.
Die-cut look: a thick white outline, a slight shadow, a glossy highlight.
Page backgrounds are plain, dotted, ruled or grid so the stickers carry the colour.
The final page is a complete collection with a star sticker signed by the giver.
watch_outs: Drag needs a tap alternative for small hands and motor difficulties. Keep stickers original: no licensed characters or brand logos. Icons are template shapes, so hold one style per card. Photo stickers of children need consent.

gender_fit: Neutral. The editor's voice is set by the giver, and old-school 'newspaperman' clichés are left out.
when_it_makes_sense: Adults and seniors who read newspapers, or who enjoy a deadpan 'local hero' joke.\nMilestone birthdays (40, 50, 60) that call for a headline.\nCards for colleagues and friends with many shared stories.
example_card_a: Gary, 60, retiring teacher, from colleagues. Broadsheet Grey palette; Old Standard TT + Libre Baskerville; front page with masthead, banner and columns; column rules and drop caps; press roll-in; tap a headline to read the story. Banner: 'LOCAL TEACHER STILL TALKING ABOUT ROCKS'.
example_card_b: Dani, 27, from her housemates. Tabloid Yellow palette; Special Elite + Courier Prime; classifieds grid; EXCLUSIVE stamps; stamp thud; cut out the coupon. Classified: 'WANTED: someone to finish the oat milk. Apply within.' Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Birthday date and place: the dateline.
Best-known trait or event: the banner headline.
The giver: the editor. Friends: correspondents.
Era of the recipient's youth: the paper's style (Victorian broadsheet, mid-century tabloid, modern digital).
Tone: straight-faced or sensational.
fixed_dna:
A masthead with an invented paper name and a dateline built from the birthday and the place.
A banner headline, a picture with a caption, and body copy with column rules and a drop cap (one column on phones).
Inside pages use newspaper furniture: letters to the editor, classifieds, a crossword, a forecast, a scoreboard.
Straight-faced news writing used for affectionate exaggeration.
watch_outs: Small serif text in columns can fail readability: body 17 px or larger and a single column on phones. Never imitate a real paper's masthead or fonts, and never mimic real news events or people. Keep headlines kind.

gender_fit: Neutral. Velvet, silver, blue, dusk, noir and popcorn palettes cover the range.
when_it_makes_sense: Film buffs, drama-loving friends, the friend who 'should have their own movie'.\nBig birthdays (40, 50, 60) that deserve a red carpet.\nA giver who wants to 'direct'.
example_card_a: Elena, 50, film buff, from her book club. Velvet & Gold palette; Limelight + Josefin Sans; marquee front with a title sign; marquee bulbs; curtain rise; take your seat. Title: 'ELENA: THE DIRECTOR'S CUT'.
example_card_b: Finn, 13, from his little sister. Drive-In Dusk palette; Cinzel + Libre Baskerville; ticket stub and seat map; popcorn, tickets and stars; credits roll; vote on the cast. Title: 'FINN 13: THE SEQUEL NOBODY ASKED FOR'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Tone and personality: genre (comedy, adventure, drama, documentary).
Their best story: the plot of the feature.
Catchphrases: the tagline.
Friends: the cast. The giver: the director.
Era of their taste: the film-stock look (silent, saturated colour, 80s, modern digital).
fixed_dna:
Opens with a marquee or curtains rising and closes with rolling credits and a post-credits scene.
Each scene is a still, poster or reel with a film-style title card and a tagline.
Letterboxed frames and cinematic type. Light comes from spotlights, projector beams and marquee bulbs.
Invented film titles and studios only: no real films, actors, studios or quotes.
watch_outs: No real films, actors, studios, awards or famous lines. Film grain and light beams lower text contrast: keep text on solid panels. Dark themes need larger text for older eyes. The credits must be skippable.

gender_fit: Neutral. Six neon pairs are in the kit, from magenta and cyan to lime and lilac.
when_it_makes_sense: Adults 30 to 50 who grew up with 80s and 90s pop culture.\nTeens who like retro-futurism, and music-led cards.\nNight owls and road-trip people.
example_card_a: Carlos, 44, road-trip fan, from his wife. Sunset Grid palette; Monoton + Space Grotesk; windshield view; grid horizon and sun stripes; road scroll; turn the key. Station 'CARLOS FM'.
example_card_b: Nia, 17, from her friends. Ice Neon palette; Bungee + Work Sans; dashboard radio with a now-playing display; stars and satellites; sun rise; change the radio station. Billboard: 'NEXT EXIT: FINALS SURVIVED'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Age and era (80s and 90s nostalgia): the grid, car and chrome.
Favourite colours: the neon pair.
Road trips and places: billboard names.
Music taste: the station and 'now playing'.
Their real vehicle (car, bike, scooter): the silhouette.
fixed_dna:
One continuous scene: the road or horizon moves forward as the recipient advances, and each scene is a stop or billboard along the route.
Neon-tube and chrome type on a dark sky, with a horizon grid, sun and stars.
A dashboard radio: the station is the card title, tracks are scenes, volume is the sound opt-in.
Light-on-dark with glow, but glow never lowers text contrast: text sits on solid panels.
watch_outs: Glow and motion can hurt legibility and trigger motion sensitivity: text on solid panels, honour reduced-motion, nothing flashing. No real car brands, songs, lyrics or logos. Check every neon colour against its panel for contrast.

gender_fit: Neutral. The engineer stereotype skews male: draw the assembly from the person's own craft (knitting, baking, dance) and use Drafting Vellum, Whiteprint or Cyanotype Green.
when_it_makes_sense: Engineers, makers, architects and DIY people.\nAnyone described as 'well built': dry-humour cards for colleagues and partners.\nA quieter alternative to Firmware for people who like drawings.
example_card_a: Hana, 36, architect, from her partner. Drafting Vellum palette; Barlow Condensed + DM Mono; floor plan of a 'home' (their life rooms); dimension lines and arrows; dimension pop; tap a callout to read its note. Room: 'Kitchen (bagels, 2 a.m.)'.
example_card_b: Ollie, 10, Lego and rockets, from his mum. Classic Blueprint palette; Architects Daughter + B612 Mono; exploded view with numbered parts; gears, bolts and fasteners; exploded view (parts drift apart); drag the exploded view apart. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Hobby or tool: the assembly being drawn (a bike, a kettle, a guitar, a heart).
Habits: tolerances and notes.
Age: the revision number.
Work or hobby: the discipline (mechanical, architectural, electrical).
Tone: how dry the notes are.
fixed_dna:
Every scene is a drawing sheet with a title block (sheet number, scale, drawn by, date) and a revision table.
Line art only: thin strokes, dimension arrows, callout bubbles and hatching, in one ink on one paper colour plus one highlight.
Technical voice: notes, tolerances, 'DO NOT SCALE'.
Drawings are inline SVG built from simple parts, never traced from photos.
watch_outs: Thin lines vanish on small phones: minimum stroke 1.5 px, tested at 320 px width. The technical voice must not swamp the affection. Keep SVG parts simple and never promise accurate engineering drawings of real objects.

gender_fit: Neutral. Six palettes run from navy and teal to kraft and sunset.
when_it_makes_sense: Travellers, expats and couples who met abroad, and friends spread across cities.\nRecipients who moved country, or who love trips.\nGifts framed as 'a journey', and milestones such as 30, 40 or 50.
example_card_a: Noor, 33, moved from Cairo to Toronto, from her sister. Passport Navy palette; Yellowtail + Josefin Sans; passport page with stamps; visa stamps; stamp thud; tap to stamp the page. Stamp: 'TORONTO: FIRST WINTER SURVIVED'.
example_card_b: Bill, 68, retired and loves the coast, from his kids. Airmail palette; Special Elite + Lora; postcard front and back; airmail stripes and postage stamps; page flip; flip the postcard. Postcard: 'Wish you were here (you always were).' Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Places they lived in, visited or dream of: destinations.
Habits: 'visa categories' (Coffee, Snacks).
Age: 'valid for N years'.
Travel taste: the look (steamship, jet-age airline, backpacker journal, road-trip motel).
fixed_dna:
Opens on a passport cover (or a boarding pass) issued to the recipient. Every scene stamps a page.
Destinations are real places from the facts, or invented places named for habits and marked as jokes. A route line links them in story order.
Ephemera are the visual language: stamps, tickets, luggage tags, postcards.
Ends on 'Arrivals: home' with the giver's message as the last postcard.
watch_outs: Never mimic a real passport, visa or border stamp closely enough to pass as official: use invented country names and layouts. Real places are facts and come only from the giver. Sensitive geography (migration, war, loss) needs a gentle tone and a skip. Maps are simple line art, not accurate borders.

gender_fit: Neutral. Stripes, bulbs and booths come from the person's own favourites.
when_it_makes_sense: Kids 5 to 12 and their parents.\nTeens and adults who love games and warm nostalgia.\nCards with several small games and a big finale, or a party-themed birthday.
example_card_a: Milo, 8, from his family. Ferris Blue palette; Chewy + Figtree; midway strip; balloons and pinwheels; prize drop; play the booth game. Booth: 'The Lego Toss'.
example_card_b: Sandra, 45, from her friends. Midway Night palette; Alfa Slab One + Work Sans; Ferris wheel with scenes as gondolas; string lights and bulbs; wheel turn; ride the wheel to the top. Booth: 'Coffee Cup Ring Toss'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Habits and obsessions: the booths (Coffee Toss, Snack Stack).
Friends: barkers and side-show performers.
Age: the 'you must be this old' sign.
Favourite colours: the stripes.
Games in the facts: which booths are playable.
fixed_dna:
Opens at the gate with an admit-one ticket for the recipient and closes at the top of the Ferris wheel or a fireworks finale.
Each scene is a booth or attraction with a hand-painted sign and a prize. Games are gentle and always won.
Sign-painter lettering, striped awnings and string lights. The barker's voice is the giver's.
Prizes are messages and badges, never invented claims about their life.
watch_outs: Games are gentle and always won. No scary clowns and no jokes about bodies. Plush and balloon shapes are original, never licensed characters. The bulb-chase animation stays brief and honours reduced-motion.

gender_fit: Neutral. Cases are about habits, not gender, and the palette range runs from manila to night.
when_it_makes_sense: Friends and colleagues who enjoy mock-serious humour, and fans of detective shows.\nCards built on habits and running jokes, or a team roasting a beloved boss.\nAdults and older teens.
example_card_a: Dee, 29, chronic latecomer, from her flatmates. Manila & Stamp palette; Special Elite + Courier Prime; folder open with clipped documents; rubber stamps; stamp thud; open the folder. Charge: 'Repeated arrival at the last minute'.
example_card_b: Uncle Ray, 62, always fixing things, from his nieces. Cosy Mystery palette; IBM Plex Mono + Lora; suspect board with photos and string; red string and pins; string draw; connect the pins. Charge: 'Possession of 14 screwdrivers, none the right one'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Habits: 'suspicious activities'.
Catchphrases: witness quotes.
Friends: witnesses and 'agents'.
Objects they carry: evidence.
Age: 'years at large'.
Tone: noir, comic procedural or cosy mystery.
fixed_dna:
Opens on a closed manila folder with a case number and closes with a 'CASE CLOSED' stamp and a verdict.
Scenes are documents: witness statements, evidence tags, a surveillance log, a suspect board with string.
Some lines are redacted, and tapping a redaction reveals a kind twist.
Typewriter and stamp lettering on manila and paper. No real agencies, forces, seals or badges.
watch_outs: Keep every offence comic and harmless: no crimes, weapons or drugs, and nothing that reads as a real accusation. No real agencies, police marks or seals. Redactions never hide something hurtful. Typewriter fonts strain reading at small sizes: body 16 px or more.

gender_fit: Neutral. Quiet by design, with palettes from white cube to plaster pink.
when_it_makes_sense: Parents and grandparents, and retrospective milestones (50, 60, 70, 80).\nPhoto-rich family cards, and quiet tasteful cards for people who would dislike a loud one.\nPartners marking a shared history.
example_card_a: Grandpa Joe, 80, from his family. Charcoal Room palette; Fraunces + Figtree; salon wall with many frames; frames and mats; slow fade between walls; tap a piece to read its label. Show: 'JOE: A RETROSPECTIVE, 1946 TO TODAY'.
example_card_b: Amara, 40, from her partner. Plaster Pink palette; Italiana + Inter; single framed piece with a wall label; abstract shapes as 'art'; frame lift; walk to the next room. Piece: 'Sunday, Slightly Burnt Toast (2019). Toast on plate.' Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Photos and objects: the pieces.
Years: rooms by decade or by theme.
Quotes: label lines.
The giver: the curator.
Tone: a reverent or a wry curatorial voice.
Number of photos: how many frames, with designed objects filling gaps.
fixed_dna:
Opens on an exhibition title wall ('NAME: A Retrospective, 1986 to today') and closes at a visitors' book.
Every scene is a wall of one to four framed pieces, each with a wall label (title, year, medium, one line).
White space, slow fades and calm pacing. Refined type with one restrained accent.
An optional audio guide narrates, but the text is always on the page.
watch_outs: White space looks empty with too little content: switch to Vitrine or Single piece layouts below 4 pieces. Never imitate real artworks, artists or museum branding. Frames need real approved photos, and the designed-object fallback must be as good. Labels stay at 16 px or larger.

gender_fit: Neutral. Menu styles run from chalkboard to diner to izakaya, all picked from the person's own tastes.
when_it_makes_sense: Foodies, home cooks, bakers and coffee people.\nDinner-party friends, or a card that arrives before a meal out.\nPartners and families who share meals.
example_card_a: Marta, 55, baker, from her family. Bistro Paper palette; Playfair Display + Lora; menu card with dotted leaders; herb, spice and fruit icons; cloche lift; lift the cloche. Dish: 'Sourdough, 1998 (the year you opened)'.
example_card_b: Jin, 22, ramen fan, from his roommates. Izakaya Night palette; Amatic SC + Nunito; chalkboard specials; chalk doodles; chalk write-on; tap the bell. Special: 'Midnight Noodles (bring a friend)'. Differs on all 6 axes.
facts_that_drive_the_look:
Food and drink they love: real dishes (only when the facts say so).
Memories: dish names.
Habits: the specials.
Taste (not heritage): menu style (bistro, izakaya, diner, bakery, chalkboard café).
Age: the 'vintage' on the pairing list.
fixed_dna:
Opens on a menu cover ('Tonight, in honour of NAME') and closes with the bill.
Scenes are courses in order: amuse-bouche (opener), starter, main, palate cleanser (a game), dessert (the heartfelt part), digestif (sign-off).
Each dish has a name, a short menu-speak description and a tasting note that carries the story.
Menu typography: small caps, dotted leaders, 'priceless' price jokes. No real restaurants, chefs or brands.
watch_outs: Only name foods and drinks the facts mention: never assume alcohol, diet or cuisine from age, culture or looks. No diet, weight or allergy jokes. No real restaurant or chef branding. Dotted leaders and small caps need larger sizes on phones.
